oneLineAnswer: Phenytoin is a prescription anti-seizure drug for epilepsy, taken long term, and it needs blood-level monitoring.
whatItIs: Phenytoin is an anti-seizure medicine, also called an antiepileptic. Chemically it sits close to the barbiturates, but it has a five-membered ring instead of their shape. Its chemical name is 5,5-diphenyl-2,4-imidazolidinedione. The formula is C15H12N2O2 and the molecular weight is 252.27. It is sold as capsules, tablets, a chewable tablet and a liquid. A version also goes into a vein.
whatItDoes: It is used for two seizure patterns: generalized tonic-clonic seizures and complex partial seizures.
It is also given to prevent and treat seizures around brain surgery.
A vein version is used for a long, unbroken seizure called status epilepticus.
Nobody knows exactly how it works. The leading idea is that it blocks sodium channels, the tiny gates nerve cells use to fire.
Blocking those gates calms the fast, repeated firing that a seizure depends on.
The helpful range and the harmful range sit close together, so blood tests are used to follow the level.
howPeopleUseIt: Most people swallow it as a capsule, tablet, chewable tablet or liquid.
Slow-release capsules are absorbed gradually, so blood levels peak about 4 to 12 hours after a swallow.
It is usually a long-term medicine rather than a short course.
Periodic blood tests check the drug level, and sometimes liver and blood counts too.
Labels say any change in amount should be gradual. Stopping suddenly can set off seizures.
The label also suggests brushing, flossing and dental visits, because the drug can overgrow the gums.
Some people stay on it for years while a clinician adjusts the amount.

commonSideEffects: The most frequent problems involve the nervous system, and they track how much drug is in the blood.
They include flickering eye movements (nystagmus), poor balance and walking (ataxia), slurred speech, clumsiness, drowsiness and confusion.
Gums can thicken and overgrow. This is called gingival hyperplasia.
Nausea, vomiting, constipation and skin rash are also reported.
Dizziness, headache, trouble sleeping, twitching and a metallic taste show up as well.
seriousSigns: Skin reactions can turn severe. Examples are Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.
A whole-body allergic reaction called DRESS can involve skin, liver, kidneys, blood, heart or lungs.
Labels ask patients to report fever, rash, swollen glands, face swelling or mouth sores.
Easy bruising, or yellowing of skin and eyes, are other things they are told to report.
The liver can be injured, which may show up as jaundice and dark urine.
Blood counts can fall, raising the chance of infection, bruising and bleeding.
The heart can beat too slowly, and rare cardiac arrest has been reported.
Labels carry a warning about suicidal thoughts and behavior.
Long-term use has been tied to weaker bones and to nerve damage in the hands and feet.
Blood sugar can rise, because the drug can reduce insulin release.
A balance centre in the brain, the cerebellum, can shrink. This has been reported with phenytoin.
whoShouldAvoid: Anyone who has reacted badly to phenytoin or to another hydantoin drug.
Anyone whose liver was injured by phenytoin in the past.
Anyone taking delavirdine, because phenytoin can stop it working.
Caution is advised with liver or kidney disease, the blood disorder porphyria, high blood sugar, or regular alcohol use.
Labels say the drug can harm an unborn baby. People who could become pregnant are told to discuss alternatives with a clinician.

interactions: Phenytoin sticks to proteins in the blood and is broken down by liver enzymes named CYP2C9 and CYP2C19.
That breakdown becomes saturated at high levels. Even a small change in amount can then push blood levels up sharply.
Phenytoin also speeds up many liver enzymes, so it can weaken other medicines.
Drugs that can raise phenytoin levels include fluconazole, ketoconazole, omeprazole, cimetidine, fluoxetine, sertraline, sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim, amiodarone, isoniazid and warfarin.
Things that can lower phenytoin levels include antacids, rifampin, diazepam and carbamazepine.
Folic acid, St John's wort and heavy long-term drinking also lower the level.
Antacids are a special case. Labels say not to take them at the same time of day.
Alcohol cuts both ways. A single drink can raise the level, while long-term drinking can lower it.
Phenytoin can make hormonal contraception work less well.
It can change warfarin's effect in either direction.
Valproate shifts phenytoin levels unpredictably, and the pair is linked to a rise in blood ammonia.
Phenytoin can weaken many other drugs, including some antifungals, HIV medicines, statins, calcium channel blockers, vitamin D and corticosteroids.
Tube feeding and liquid nutrition can cut how much phenytoin is absorbed.
pregnancyAndChildren: During pregnancy phenytoin may raise the risk of birth defects, including cleft lip or palate and heart defects. A pattern of abnormalities called fetal hydantoin syndrome has also been reported. Pregnancy can lower drug levels in the blood, so seizures may become harder to control. Babies exposed before birth can have a bleeding problem. It comes from low levels of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors. The label says vitamin K can prevent it. A pregnancy registry tracks outcomes for people who take anti-seizure drugs. Children may be given chewable tablets or oral liquid. Older adults clear the drug more slowly, and the label says this can change dosing.
whatWeDoNotKnow: How often each side effect happens is not known. Labels collect voluntary reports, so they cannot give reliable frequencies.
The exact way phenytoin stops seizures has never been established.
The labels do not put a number on how often serious liver injury occurs.
Whether testing for CYP2C9 gene variants improves outcomes is not settled by these sources.
Effects on memory and thinking across many years are not fully described in the labels.
How phenytoin compares with newer anti-seizure drugs is outside what these sources cover.

gaps: LiverTox (NIDDK) has a phenytoin record at https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548889/. The NCBI Bookshelf refused every fetch with a reCAPTCHA bot check. No LiverTox fact is cited, so the record carries no liver-injury frequency estimate.
https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/phenytoin returned HTTP 404. NCCIH appears to publish no phenytoin page, so no NCCIH content is cited.
MedlinePlus drug monographs were excluded on purpose. NLM states they are copyrighted American Society of Health-System Pharmacists content.

The two label sources (openFDA and DailyMed) publish the same underlying FDA prescribing information. They are different publishers and pages, but not fully independent of each other for safety detail.
Liver-injury frequency is missing. LiverTox would have supplied it, and the labels do not state a rate.
Relative benefit versus newer anti-seizure drugs is not covered. No systematic review or head-to-head outcome data was fetched.
Side-effect frequencies are absent. The labels state that voluntary reports come from a population of uncertain size, so rates cannot be calculated.
Approval history is not covered. Sources found for the 1946 US approval and yearly prescription counts were in the unfetchable LiverTox record.
Product-level differences were not compared. That includes inactive ingredients in specific capsules and tablets. openFDA returns about 40 oral and 49 injectable label records.
No pediatric dosing detail is given. Chewable and liquid forms exist for children. Dose content is out of scope for this record.
summary: This record covers phenytoin's identity, approved uses, monitoring, risks, interactions and remaining gaps.
